caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No 1979 of 2001
lawyer:
AJ Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate, instructed by Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioners. 
Not represented—The Respondents.
parties:
Ambiya Khatun & ors ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Noor Ahmed & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal is against the judgment and order dated August 20, 2001 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1708 of 1997 making the Rule absolute obtained against the judgment and order dated January 19, 1997 of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Brahmanbaria, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 1993 allowing the same upon reversing the judgment and order dated November 23, 1992 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 9 of 1990 (under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950) allowing the prayer for pre-emption. 

 2. Pre-emptor-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act seeking pre-emption as co-sharer in respect of the transfer made by kabala dated 18-1-1990 against the petitioners herein contending that they are stranger purchasers in the holding land of which sought to be pre-empted. 

 9. The learned Advocates for the petitioner submits that the land sought to be pre-empted as has gone back to the co-sharer vendor and, as such, if pre-emption is allowed the same would result in depriving the co-sharer of his property. The learned Counsel also submits as re-conveyance took place before the expiry of the time prescribed by law for filing an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act no exception ought to have been taken to the re-conveyance so made and prayer for pre-emption ought to have been rejected. He lastly submits that there are two reported cases one in 37 DLR 324 and another in 47 DLR 607 taking divergent view as to whether re-conveyance during the pendency of the Miscellaneous Case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is hit by the provision of section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 11. The other contention of the learned Counsel that as the land has gone back to the vendor during the pendency of the Miscellaneous Case and consequently, there being no transaction for pre-emption, the judgment of the High Court Division allowing pre-emption would amount to deprive the co-sharer-vendor of his land which he got back upon re-conveyance. In the case of Shaft Khan vs. Mannujan Hussain reported in 35 DLR (AD) 225 in the background of the facts that land sought to be pre-empted was sold on 28-3-1974 and re-conveyance took place on 31-10-1974 and the Miscellaneous. Case seeking pre-emption was filed on 1-11-1974 it has been held "the right to pre-emption is therefore not available as the original vendor and co-sharer got back already his ownership in its entirety, it being immaterial whether he got back his ownership in pursuance of an agreement for re-conveyance or independent of any such agreement. The main question for careful examination will be, whether he actually got back his land, and if the answer is in the affirmative, the position will be as if no transfer was at all made by him. If, however, it is found that the re-sale is a colourable show-up or a mere paper transaction and that right, title and interest in the land have not gone back to the vendor but still remain vested in the transferee then the re-sale may be ignored and preemption may be allowed." In the instant case it has been found by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court that the agreement on the basis of which re-conveyance took place was a collusive one. This being the position we are of the view that whatever transaction took place between the pre-emptees and their vendor was product of collusion and the transaction is tainted with fraud and the said transaction was made collusively and fraudulently by the pre-emptee and the original vendor only to defeat the claim of the pre-emptor. In our view, the re-conveyance transaction being tainted with fraud and collusion the same can in no way deprive the pre-emptor from his claim of pre-emption and in a case like the instant one if the pre-emption is rejected that would amount to giving premium to the fraudulent and collusive transaction between the original owner and the pre-emptee. The other contention that re-conveyance took place before the expiry of the period prescribed in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act i.e. expiry of the period of 4 months, the High Court Division was in error in allowing the prayer for pre-emption upon setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court. The person seeking pre-emption may file an application under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act within 4 months as mentioned therein. The law is settled now that the right of pre-emption accrues on the registration of the kabala sought to be pre-empted. It is seen from the judgment of the trial Court that the kabala sought to be pre-empted was entered in the volume as per provision of section 60 of the Registration Act on 17-2-1990 and the Miscellaneous Case was filed on 13-3-1990. So, it is evident that Miscellaneous Case seeking pre-emption was filed when the right to pre-empt accrued. The law is not that a person seeking pre-emption is to file the Miscellaneous Case on the last day of 4 months as in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, rather it is the option of the pre-emptor at what point of time he would file the application under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or, in other words, whether on the very day right to pre-emption has accrued or on the last day on the expiry whereof pre-emptor's right of pre-emption would be barred by limitation. We have already noticed that Miscellaneous Case was filed on 13-3-1990 seeking pre-emption of the transfer that was made by the kabala dated 18-1-1990 and was registered on 17-2-1990 and the re-conveyance took place on 28-3-1990. So, the contention that exception ought not to have been taken in respect of the re-conveyance which took place before the expiry of time prescribed by law for seeking pre-emption is of no substance.
